utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're waiting for that, there is a short matter that I can report to the Chamber, if it pleases the Court, now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so if we can deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, yesterday 65 ter 10822 was marked as P15 and marked for identification because the Defence objected to the admission of this document as an exhibit because it is in English yet purports to be authored by General Dragomir Milosevic. I think it is most appropriate to lead evidence on it with an upcoming witness. So at this stage the Prosecution will not move forward with the tendering but will lead additional evidence to explain the circumstances as to why it's in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We will then wait for that witness to appear and P15 remains marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Schmitz, I take it. Ms. Schmitz, before you give evidence the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Schmitz. Please be seated. You'll first be examined by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us your name, please.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: My name is Christine Schmitz.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you recently testified in the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes, I did, end of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you've had a chance to look at your -- what we've referred to and is marked as the amalgamated statement for this case?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, that is 65 ter 28321.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is it true and correct to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: It is true and correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if you were asked about that information, would you be giving the same answers related to that information?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer that statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Petrusic will cross-examine this witness so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He will deal with the rest of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections against the statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted. No objections. Madam Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 10638 becomes Exhibit P27, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P27 is admitted into evidence. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second. That's the wrong --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number is wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The number is wrong. Madam Registrar, would you please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number -- document number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: -- 10638 becomes Exhibit P27, Your Honours. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's supposed to be document 28321.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document -- I apologise, Your Honours. Document 28321 becomes Exhibit P27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P27 is now for the third time admitted into evidence. It is undated, the amalgamated statement of Ms. Schmitz. Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And now I'll read a summary of that statement for everyone. Christine Schmitz is a qualified nurse. She first began her work with the NGO Doctors Without Borders, known as MSF, in 1991. In her work as a nurse for MSF, she's worked around the world in places as Somalia, Iraq, Liberia, Sudan, and Chechnya. On June 24th, 1995, Ms. Schmitz arrived in Srebrenica in the enclave belong with her MSF colleague, Dr. Daniel O'Brien. Ms. Schmitz took up the post of field co-ordinator for the MSF project in the Srebrenica enclave, basically in charge of that project. The project had been up and running and was centred upon offering medical care to the population of the enclave. Ms. Schmitz monitored the MSF medical programme in Srebrenica and supervised the local staff. Along with her medical duties, Ms. Schmitz had responsibility for security issues, liaison with local authorities, other NGOs, and the Dutch Battalion, known as DutchBat. She made regular reports via telex to MSF in Belgrade. She lived in a house next to the hospital near the centre of Srebrenica town. After her arrival, Ms. Schmitz was informed by UNHCR and the local authorities that there was a shortage of food in the enclave and that some people were suffering from starvation. MSF in Belgrade had informed her that the Bosnian Serbs were refusing to allow regular food and medical convoys to the enclave. On July 6th there was a definite change in the situation in Srebrenica and she was awakened by heavy shelling that sounded close to the town but not in the town itself. She moved to the bunker under the hospital. During the following days, a pattern developed of periods of heavy shelling in and around the town interspersed with periods of quiet. Due to the shelling, an increased number of shelling victims were brought to the hospital for treatment. By 10 July the hospital was so full of wounded that the doctors had difficulty coping. On the 10th, shells began landing in town, including right across the street from the hospital. The population of Srebrenica was extremely frightened and seeking protection with the UN forces. The local Muslim medical staff feared for the patients and wanted to evacuate them and spoke of atrocities at the Vukovar Hospital earlier in the war. On 11 July the local population left towards the Dutch base in Potocari. The local doctors at the hospital decided to evacuate the patients and move everyone to Potocari due to the increasing danger, and Ms. Schmitz and Dr. O'Brien accepted that. Ms. Schmitz and others joined a large number of Muslims walking up the road to Potocari. She could hear shells exploding close to the road as they walked. She reached the UN compound in Potocari that afternoon and by the evening of 11 July estimated about 20.000 Muslims had assembled in the area around the UN base. As she walked through the crowd of Muslims that evening, she noticed shells frequently exploding in the vicinity and people were sitting in the open air shivering with fear and begging her to take them inside the UN enclave. On 12 July she supervised the set-up of medical treatment tents by DutchBat across the street from the UN compound. While arranging this she met briefly with the local Muslim logistics officer named Meho. She implored him to come to the compound with her for his personal safety and to assist in the sanitation system. But he refused in order to stay with his family and she's not seen him since that time. At about noon Ms. Schmitz was informed by DutchBat that General Mladic wanted to begin evacuating the sick and wounded Muslims. She objected to this as the patients were her responsibility and she did not think it was right to turn them over to the Bosnian Serbs for transport. She sought out General Mladic and found him just outside the compound gates where she spoke to him briefly on the matter. During the day she drove up and down the main road looking for patients. During this time she noticed mainly women and children and some old men being loaded onto buses and she was told people were being separated, though she did not see this at this point. She did notice that people were exhausted and frightened and desperate to leave. That evening, sometime before 9.00 p.m., she continued to drive along the road seeking out patients. At this point she again encountered General Mladic and sought his permission to continue her search and the General agreed she could. On the 13th of July, the transportation of the local population continued. A Muslim man followed by a Serb soldier with a rifle approached Ms. Schmitz and handed her his baby. The man was crying and very frightened. Ms. Schmitz also witnessed that day the beating of a Muslim man by Bosnian Serb soldiers. From the 14th to the 17th, much of her time was spent negotiating for the evacuation of MSF patients and their local staff. MSF had seven local male workers and one local female interpreter working for them. On 17 July, the MSF patients were evacuated safely by the ICRC from the enclave. On 21 July Ms. Schmitz, Dr. O'Brien, and eight local staff and five of their relatives, along with two patients, were allowed to leave the enclave and travel to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that a correct summary of some of what you have told us in your statement?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, two observations. First, the summary, three full pages, the Chamber had in mind close to one page. So it's a very extensive summary. Could you please keep that in mind. Second, it's just for the public, so whether the summary is accurate or not of course is not for the witness because the summary is not evidence. The evidence is the statement, nothing more, nothing less. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we can go over a couple of the points that were brought up just to provide some context and some clarification. When you mention that on 10 July the hospital was so full of wounded that there was difficulty coping, can you give us a rough estimate of, you know, how many wounded or injured people there were in the hospital at that point?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Well, I think the hospital was not totally full yet at that time. It had not been full at all before the bombing started. I think the main issue about not coping was that we did only have one national surgeon who was totally overworked. We were not allowed to have an international surgeon who would have been very helpful at this time, so he was only able to operate on one patient at a time assisted by another general practitioner. So patients being brought in, for example, suffering of shrapnel wounds could not be taken care of in case they needed an operation because he was only able to work on one patient. So they were laying patients everywhere in the corridors. There was one truck who was still functioning and did have fuel, so -- this truck had a special horn, and when we did hear the horn - and we did hear that often - then we knew more patients were coming in. The hospital was totally full but also with relatives and friends who were worried about the wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Schmitz, sorry to interrupt, but would you please focus your answer on the question because you have now explained why there was only one doctor. The simple question was whether you give an estimate of the number of wounded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And injured people in the hospital, and we are limited in our time. Yes, please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, roughly how many people was that, if you recall? Just your best estimate.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: My best estimate would be 50 to 60 patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who were these folks? Were they -- were there able-bodied men among them? Were there any women and children? Just can you give us a description of who they were and what kind of injuries they had? Just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: There were women and children among the patients, but the bigger part were young men who were being brought from the centre and the surrounding.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what were their injuries, basically?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Most of the injuries were results from the bombings, so shrapnel wounds, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And you had told us in your statement that the doctor, the local doctors, were afraid and wanted to move the patients out and mentioned something about Vukovar Hospital. What were your understanding of what this reference to Vukovar hospital was?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know all the details, but I had understood or I just knew that in Vukovar years earlier, some 200 patients had been just killed in the hospital beds and this is what local doctors wanted to avoid and therefore bring them to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was there any knowledge with you at the time on who allegedly had killed the patients of the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: No, not exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know which side, which army, if anyone, or was it just unknown?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: No, that was not known to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And as you were going up towards Potocari with the crowd, you said you could hear shells exploding close to the road. Can you describe that briefly and what you made of those shells exploding close to the road?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Well, it -- to me it appeared as if the shells were supposed to fall like this, that the crowd did stay on the road and did not try -- the people did not try to escape, but that was my feeling. I understood it like this, we should stay on the road and nobody was supposed to escape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us how you got that feeling? That's hard to imagine.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: It's -- okay. Difficult to explain. And it was not so that the shell was exploding right close to a person but maybe 5 to 10 metres further, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now you also said that when you were walking around the compound, the local Muslims were shivering with fear. What do you mean by that? Can you just describe that? Try to put us there briefly.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Well, that was the time of the 11th and 12th, 11th especially, in the evening when all the displaced had arrived in Potocari. They were just sitting and shivering with fear when the shells were falling and very afraid and trembling and very -- also in apathetic state, they were basically shocked not knowing what was going to happen, so they were very desperate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where were these shells falling at this point, as far as you could make out?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Again, certainly shells were falling around Potocari, around the compound, around the place, outside the UN compound where the displaced were just sitting on the ground. Given that I was then in Potocari, I don't know if more shells were falling in Srebrenica itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now let's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, could I seek clarification of one of the previous answers. You said: "It was not that the shell was exploding right close to a person but maybe 5 to 10 metres further, exactly." Do I understand that the persons you refer to were persons on the road --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and that the shells fell within 5 to 10 metres, so immediately next to the road? Is that -- 5 to 10 metres -- 5 metres is the distance between you and me at this moment. Was it that close?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was that close, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: None of the shells hit the road ever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not when I was present and on the road with the population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How many shells did you see falling within such a short distance from the road? Was it one or ten or 50, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is difficult to say because I was not always watching when the shells were falling, but just rather trying to look ahead because we were driving behind a walking population. I did more hear them. So on the way down to Potocari -- it's difficult for me to say if it were two or 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was it by sound that you determined that they were falling within 5 or 10 metres or did you -- I mean, if a shell falls at such a short distance, you would expect more than just to hear the sound but also to see something, dust -- well, you may be better aware of how an explosion looks but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was mostly by hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next day, on the 12th of July, that's a day when the Bosnian Serb army arrived. And you mentioned that you sought out General Mladic to speak to him about what you'd heard was his plan, to remove your patients. And what time -- roughly what time of day did you search out General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: That was around noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you find him?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes, I did -- well, I did not go on my own, but I did go with one of the UN liaison team, whose name I don't remember or maybe even never knew, and he was just outside the compound on the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, who was?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Ratko Mladic, together with his interpreter, was outside of the UN compound just on the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you describe the scene at that time that you saw General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: It was very crowded, very hot. He was walking down towards me, although not on purpose I believe towards me but just that direction, so I went to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did he have anyone with him?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yeah, he did have an interpreter with him, a young guy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic was wearing camouflage, so a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what happened?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Well, I did go up to him and introduced myself, who we were, what our work was in Srebrenica, and I did also explain to him that we would be also working on -- in other areas, supporting Serbian population. And then I said that I had heard that he had wanted to evacuate the patients and that I would strongly object against it, that I would feel it would be the responsibility of MSF to organise the evacuation and not the BSA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was his response, if any?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Well, I do not know what his response was because he did speak in Serbo-Croatian, but his translator, his interpreter, just told me that I should go and do my job and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall the General's physical expression, attitude towards you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I had the feeling that I was disturbing him. He wasn't interested in what I had to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What gave you that feeling?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: He did not really react on what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how were you able to conclude this was General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I knew him from before from different media broadcasts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And when did the -- did the patients actually get evacuated first, as you heard was going to happen?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And just remind us, when did the -- your patients actually get evacuated?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: On the 17th of July, in the evening, by ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And did you again see General Mladic that evening?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes, I did see General Mladic on the 12th of July, in the evening, around 9.00, when I was again outside among the displaced looking for patients. I saw him and I had the feeling that there was a question in his face like: What is she doing here? And so together with my female interpreter, Amira, I went up to him and requested to be allowed to pick up sick and wounded and he agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we go to 65 ter 28323. Do you recall making a rough sketch of the Potocari area, the UN compound?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That was 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that should hopefully come up on the screen. Is this your sketch?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And there should also be -- I believe there's a translation of it, though it's pretty clear. We see "Bratunac" in the top. I don't know if we catch the whole bottom of that. Maybe we make it a little smaller because I think there's Srebrenica in the arrow towards the bottom. And DutchBat compound, is that the rough triangle to the right of the picture?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: That's a kind of square, different -- there were different buildings, so it's really a rough sketch.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And these parallel lines in the middle, what is that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: The one going up to Bratunac is the street that was Tarmac, and horizontal to that didn't mean anything. That was on the right side but also some on the left side where the big groups of displaced people just sitting on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And the -- there's a triangles and I think you've marked tents there for your -- that's where you set up your medical area?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes -- well, that was the beginning. We didn't use them at all in the end because -- yeah, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Tents where, Mr. McCloskey? I can't read the writing here, it's too small.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There's a pen, she'll show you -- someone will show you how to write, and if you could circle the area of the tents.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: So opposite the Dutch compound I had requested some UN soldiers to put up some tents which I had wanted to use for triage, to see patients, so these were three tents from the UNPROFOR who set it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see, for the record, she's circled that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I know this is not -- this is not to scale, but can you see about the area where you first had that brief meeting with General Mladic about the transport of the patients? And if you could put an M there if you can identify where you first ran into him.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: It's here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, I'd offer this exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic. Mr. Mladic, no. One second, please. If you want to discuss anything with counsel, it's better -- your voice is very loud if your earphones are still in. We can even hear through our -- yes, you would like to consult for a second with Mr. Lukic. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, can we continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. First I would like to seek one clarification of one of the answers and then we'll deal with the marked sketch. Ms. Schmitz, you told us about the first encounter you had with Mr. Mladic. Then you were asked when did your patients actually get evacuated? You said on the 17th of July in the evening by the ICRC. Then the next question was: "All right. And did you again see General Mladic that evening?" Your answer was: "Yes, I did see General Mladic on the 12th of July in the evening." Mr. McCloskey was not entirely clear whether that evening was the evening of the 12th of July or of the 17th of July. Did I understand your testimony well that you did again see Mr. Mladic in the evening of the 12th of July but not on the 17th of July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I met him twice on the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. McCloskey, "that evening" is asking for confusion. It has been clarified. Any objection against the admission into evidence of the sketch? May I take it you would be happy with the sketch as marked by the witness or do you need two versions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think just one marked is fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Petrusic, no objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28323, marked by the witness, becomes Exhibit P28, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P28 is admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Ms. Schmitz, we can see that you've got a binder of things in front of you that you've glanced at a bit. Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: These are mainly all the Telexes. Most of them I had sent to our team in Belgrade and there are a few whom I received back. I didn't rescue all of them, but the ones I wrote I have them with me here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And if you need to take a look at those to refresh your recollection or help answer a question, just let us know and I think that should be fine. In fact, now I just want to go over a few of those to give us a feeling about the kind of things you were reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So could we go to 65 ter 19814.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we'll see there is an original -- that is not what I've got.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, it's page 3 in e-court -- in the English and 1 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, you can see from this that we have somehow got a copy that has a marking on it over the -- over certain part of it. Do you have -- can you, first of all, tell us what this is?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: This is the first Telex which I wrote on the 6th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we don't see the 6th of July written anywhere there. Where would the -- is that written on that document somewhere?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: You mean on my document?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So the one on the screen. Good question.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Well, it's under the mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And what time of day is it from the document itself? Can we tell?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: It's 4.52 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we see that on the Telex. All right. And this is where you say that: "... since 45 minutes heavy shelling of the surrounding of the town, not in the town itself." Is that a true and correct communication to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: That is my true communication, but of course it was judging by hearing where the shells were falling. I couldn't get any more confirmation on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you say that you're dismantling the radio and will go to the shelter, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Well, that means that in -- that's the security who were with MSF, if there's bombing, you should seek protection in a bunker so -- and the radio, we did need to keep up the communication with Belgrade. So I took the radio and Daniel and myself went into the bunker.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer that document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, before we further discuss this document, this document is in e-court 1 out of 75 pages. You just want this page?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I've decided just to take a few examples and not have the entire collection unless --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then this should be newly uploaded. We can't just admit 1 out of 75 pages into evidence. A new upload exercise has to be done. This brings me to my second point. The witness said that the date is under the marking. Now, I do understand, first of all, the marking does not appear at all in the B/C/S translation. It's just as if it says "UTC Vri jeme" and then gives the time. Now if you carefully look at it, the last two digits of what seems to be under the marking seems to be 06, which would be perhaps in accordance with the date the witness gave us. Is there any version where by copying -- any version where the original can be looked at so that we know what is under the marking? Because that usually disappears if you start colouring or marking. Is there any better version of it? Perhaps the witness would know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I asked that same question of the OTP and the answer was no, but I did not go to the witness for that, so perhaps --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The originals are with me and they are not marked, but they are not here in The Hague. They are in Berlin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any way that you could provide even copies of the unmarked versions would reveal the date again. Is there any way that -- for example, that this one, perhaps you write down which one it is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- be sent to the Office of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I have a pen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if we -- if the witness has a piece of paper and a pen so that she can write down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. McCloskey, please keep this in your mind. We can't mark it identification because then we'll have had the whole 75 pages, so please reorganise your exhibits in such a way that we later can discuss the -- either the marking for identification or admission into evidence of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Ms. Stewart's got me on -- in control on that right now, so we should be there soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we'll hear from you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to another one. 65 ter 19814, it should be page 5 in e-court. It's English page 5 and B/C/S page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's another wrong -- mistake. 19814, we've just finished with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- again, that's now page 5 out of the 75 pages? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, these are all from the same 65 ter number, which was -- created a bit of the issue before. So I'll just go to the e-court page and sort this out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And there's no problem with it -- the date. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, do you recognise this?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Sure, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what is it?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Well, it's one of my next Telexes on the 6th of July after the security meeting which usually was taking place in Srebrenica at 10.00. So usually after the meeting I went home and sent to the team in Belgrade the key issues. So if you read security: 5th of July, indicators of the attack, et cetera, that were not my information but this information came from the security meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us, was this security meeting a regular meeting?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes, it was a daily meeting in the P TT meeting opposite the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who took part in these regular meetings?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: So one person of DutchBat usually took part; one or two UNMOs, United Nations Military Observers; sometimes the national staff of ICRC; sometimes the national staff of UNHCR; and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And in looking at this we see: "6/7 0.30 a.m. six rockets at UNPROFOR compound (two exploded)." Can you tell us what that 6/7 means, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: That's the date. That happened in that morning, according to the security meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I sometimes confuse dates. Can you just confirm what this -- what actual dates these are?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: It does mean 6th of -- the information from the security meeting was that on the same day, 6th of July, 30 minutes after midnight, six rockets at UNPROFOR compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, do you know or recall which UNPROFOR compound received these rockets?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: It was the UNPROFOR compound in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is there another UNPROFOR compound?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: There was a much smaller one called Bravo Company, which was approximately 1 kilometre further from the hospital towards the north. So between Potocari and the hospital there was Bravo Company. If they would have fallen there, we would have heard them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I will also be offering this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go to another one of your documents. This is e-court page 22, the same 65 ter number, page 7 in the B/C/S. We can again see this is from you. Is this another one of your Telexes, this time dated the 10th of July?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I still haven't found it, 10.55. Yes, I did find it and indeed it's a Telex of myself to UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that is UNPROFOR in the enclave, DutchBat UNPROFOR; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes, at Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see that you conclude here -- well you say in the first sentence that: "... now the surrounding of the hospital and our house are being targeted by the shells." Can you tell us upon which -- what observations or information you made that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Well, this Telex was triggered by the fact that one shell fell and exploded right across the hospital which -- or towards our bunker, so it was extremely close. And in general the bombing had concentrated on the centre, so the danger of the shells falling came closer towards us. But the most - how to say? - impressive or shocking was the shell across the hospital and I was -- after it had exploded I ran there to see if people were wounded, which were not, but I could see the crater of it and the windows were broken in the hospital from this explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us how you were first aware of the explosion? Which of your senses caught this explosion?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I was in the bunker and I heard an enormous noise - that was the explosion. And my first thought was: This could have been just in front of the bunker and I would be trapped, so it shocked me and I was trembling with fear a second. So -- but then I realised I could still go outside and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when did you go outside?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Maybe a minute after.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you see?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I did run outside and did see the crater opposite the road -- no, not opposite the road, opposite the hospital, opposite our bunker where the shell had exploded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you give us again your best estimate in metres how far this crater was from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Maybe 10 to 15 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again, you can use the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us what, in your estimate, is the width of this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm just trying. Well, if I would be where the person is sitting until the wall there, is that 15 metres approximately? That was approximately the distance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now there are many persons seated there. May I take it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first person to me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the lady -- the lady closest to you, and then --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is only one lady.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first lady.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the second row in the courtroom on the Defence side, 15 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now can we go to one more of the communications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, perhaps one question. The hospital was not hit; is that correctly understood.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The hospital was not hit itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd like to go to -- I have 19832, it's page 1 in e-court in English. And we'll see a date of this - to help you - it should be the 10th of July. And this is, according to the document, to you and Daniel, and we see: "From Bene, Pitou, and Stef." Can you tell us what this is, this document to you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: This is a Telex from the team in Belgrade. Bene was the administrator, Pitou the logistician, and Stefan the head of mission. And they tried to cheer us up a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can see that. Now, you note that -- or, excuse me, they note that: "As we said on the radio, we agree with your analysis on your security conditions ..." What is this reference to the radio? Can you explain to us your communication ability on radio?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I do not remember on what these exactly was the response. I can only imagine. I mean we spoke every day. At the time of the 10th of July, we tried to stay as much in the bunker, but in quiet times Daniel went into the hospital to help. I did go to the security meetings. Sometimes we went to the house to have a shower. Also security --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, just -- sorry for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But just the radio, what kind of radio communications did you have? This is the first we've seen a reference to communication by radio.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I never know the name in English for what we use in German. I know only the name "radio." Maybe Mr. Fluegge can help. "Ein Funkgeraet." I don't know if there is any other expression in English for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's fine. We'll work with that. But was it a two-way radio?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where were you able to use it from? Did it -- operate it out of the bunker or did you have to go somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: We could operate from the bunker, it was possible. We had -- earlier we had used it in the house, there was an antenna, and we could operate it in the bunker. And later on in Potocari we did have a radio in the car, so we were able to use it there only in the car because nothing was installed in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, before you continue, may I ask you for a clarification, Ms. Schmitz. On page 26, lines 3 and 4, you told us who these three people are, Bene, Pitou, and Stef, but it was not correctly recorded. Bene was the administrator; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Benedict was her real name. She was the administrator in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And who was Pitou?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pitou was a nickname of Eric, who was the logistician. And Stef was the abbreviation of Stefan who was the head of mission in Belgrade, so basically my superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Just looking briefly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, I'm very sorry, "the head of mission" instead of "liaison." It should read "head of mission" in line 17 of page 27. Is that correct, head of mission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Head of mission, yes. Not liaison. I haven't said that at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we have it now. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just taking a look at paragraph 4 here, I won't read it all out, but there's a mention that they believe it's important that you agree with UNPROFOR to have regular contact and that they go on to say that it would be good to ask them if they would be ready to come and pick you up. Did that ever happen, where UNPROFOR actually agreed to come pick you up?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: They did agree to pick us up but it was not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You walked?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: No, we -- we took three of our -- well, we took all of our cars, which were three.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll also be offering that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a one-page document. No objections. 19832. Madam Registrar, the number would be ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 19832 becomes Exhibit P29, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P29 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we now go to 65 ter 28064 -- sorry that should be 65. I misread that. So it's 28065, sorry. Can you just tell us -- I mean, we see what it says this is, but in your experience did you see any cards like this?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes, I did. This is a typical old ID card of MSF, old because it did have the former logo on it, the cross, whilst nowadays we have a human being as a logo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you recognise this person?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: It's difficult to say because the last time when I was here I saw that ID card as well, and I know who the person is, Meho, but also last time I did say I would not have recognised him if I would just have seen it out of the blue. I did not know Meho well, I saw him only very briefly only twice in the time I was in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And has someone told you that this picture is Meho?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is that the Meho that you refer to in your statement, the person that you implored to get -- to come into the base but he stayed with his family?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, may I ask you for what purposes, to give us an example of an ID card or to give us Meho? Because the witness said that she was unable to see whether this was him and that she was told it was him, so for that purposes I would be hesitant to accept it as evidence but -- or is it just to give an example of an ID card; and then, of course, what's the relevance of knowing -- does it play any role anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can ask one more question and then perhaps that will answer and I can also answer your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you received information of where -- if Meho's remains were ever recovered?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes, I understood that Meho had been killed and found in a mass grave and then the ID card was also found. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that already in the statement, Mr. ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You know, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I believe it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not -- okay, but -- okay, even having heard the answer to that question, what is the probative value of this document? Is it about identity cards or is it about a person being recognised by the witness, where the witness said, I would not have recognised him but I was told that it was him?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we -- you will hear or there will be part of the record evidence of the exhumation of this man and this was recovered in the exhumation. It will help with proof of death, it will help build context and tie into her testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That clarifies everything for me. It is an ID card of which you'll later prove it was found with a certain person in a mass grave. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Any objections against admission? If not, Madam Registrar, the number would be ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28065 becomes Exhibit P30, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the last subject I want to ask you briefly about is you mention in your statement that you spent some time before leaving the enclave and negotiating for the evacuation of the wounded and your local staff. Can you tell us how many local staff you had working for you at the time in the enclave?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Well, we did have 13 local staff working for us, so drivers, interpreters, cooks, cleaners, staff, which was not having anything to do medical programme. Eight of these staff were staying with us in the UN compound. Meho we just spoke about, and the remaining staff did choose their own way to leave Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And could we go to 65 ter number 21103D. It should be e-court page 1 in the English. And this is, as you have been told, an intercept conversation that the Bosnian army intercepted, according to the Prosecution this is from -- intercept between VRS participants. And I just want to ask you if you recognise any of the names on this intercept. The first page we see a Djurdjic, a Colonel Djurdjic, does that name ring any bells for you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Jankovic, does that mean anything for you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as we go to the bottom of the page, we see there's the name clearly "Kristina" and then "(SSmit?)" meaning that it's not clear exactly what word that is, and then we see below that also a question mark "Daniel O'Brien." I take it that those names are familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's myself and Daniel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And let's go to the next page if we can. And again, I'm really interested in the content at this point, but we do see a reference in the middle of the page to the Koljevic government. Does this name "Koljevic" mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Well, I understood that this was a professor in Pale where my head of mission in Belgrade did have contact with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And do you recall any contact that your head of office had at this time-period, this July, this intercept is from 19 July 1995, as we can see from the original, the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: No, I do not recall any contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And if we look down the intercepts, we see names Abdulah Kurtovic, Ibrahim Ibrahimovic and others. Do any of those names -- do you remember any of those names?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes, very well. Abdulah Kurtovic was our cook; Ibrahim, our house keeper; Muhidin, the assistant logistician; Muhamed the logistician; Sahim [phoen], assistant logistician; and three drivers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were those all males?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Within the ages of 18 to 60?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes, and it's seven. It's the seven male staff being with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this into evidence, though of course there will be more evidence on intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 21103D becomes Exhibit P31, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. You're talking about an intercept. Would the audio be included?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, just the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. This is one of the large collections of Srebrenica intercepts where there is not audios. There are some but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for me to know. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And lastly I'd like to go to 65 ter number 05817 and this has been under seal, so if we could just not broadcast it. I believe the original is in B/C/S on your left and we have an English translation. We see here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, there's no need to go into private session for -- if it's under seal, then of course the testimony itself could also reveal -- I do not know exactly why it is under seal, but please think about it carefully, and I expect you to ask for private session if you think that apart from the document, also the questions and answer could reveal anything which should not be revealed to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I think we're going to be able to have this unsealed. This had slipped through the cracks of the document, but out of an abundance of caution we'll take care.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you seen this document before? It's dated 19 July, the same date as that intercept?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I think I saw it before when I was here in March but I do not have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And could you just take a look at those names and if we could just briefly allow her to go through that to see the names.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Well, it's basically our Belgium office who is sending a list of the national staff to the 2nd Corps of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And are those the same people you just saw mentioned in that intercept?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes. I -- so far I do see only four --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could get on to the next --

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: -- but I believe there must come more. So until number 8 it's the national staff. Number 10 is the wife of our logistician, number 11 the son of our logistician. I believe number 9 is the mother of our logistician, number 12 is the son of our driver, number 13 is the son of our driver, and then 14, 15 are the two old patients who had been found later after the 13th of July and we were requested to take them, so we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you have anything to do with the drafting of the receipt of this particular letter?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Not at all -- well, I did forward all the names to Belgrade, so the information basically came from Srebrenica from MSF.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ever give any of these names of the staff to the Bosnian Serb army folks?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes, we did give a list of the staff. I would have to consult my own papers when we did that exactly, to whom. On top of my head, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. If perhaps you could do that at the break and tell that to us. And I also forgot to mention, do you still work for MSF?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: No, I don't. I stopped in 2007.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where do you work now?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I'm working in mobile palliative care. I now work as a volunteer with the Jesuit Refugee Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where is that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: That's in Berlin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So no Syria, no Libya anymore?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I would love to, but at present I do have family reasons why I have to stay, and I must say I'm exhausted after 15 different projects with MSF in acute war situations, so I need a rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have nothing further though I would like to offer this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the -- under seal. Any objection against the letter containing a list of names? Madam Registrar, the number would be ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 05817 becomes Exhibit P32, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence under seal. Mr. Petrusic, I'm wondering, we could either take an early break and then start cross-examination after the break or you could start now, have another 12 to 13 minutes, and then continue after the break. What's your preference?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, General Mladic would prefer to have the break now for health reasons I've been told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, as far as health reasons are concerned, at this moment there's nothing on our desk which supports that apart from what Mr. Mladic feels. Now, I have no problem in taking the break at this very moment, but if you'd think that there is a health problem, then that break should be used also to verify that to the extent possible. Could you or Mr. Lukic then inform Madam Registrar whether there's anything which would need medical attention because then it should be done immediately and without delay. We take a break and we'll resume at a quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we start the cross-examination, could I hear from the -- from you, Mr. McCloskey, whether 19814, the various documents, one starting at page 3, one starting at page 5, one starting at page 7, whether they have been uploaded as separate documents, and could you then provide the 65 ter numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have not gotten that far yet --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- but we will pull them out individually and get them numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll hear from you. Please report once that's done, when they are uploaded and released. Then, Mr. Petrusic, if the witness comes in are you ready to cross-examine the witness? Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just one thing I wanted to mention, Ms. Schmitz' statement that came into evidence, it - as you'll see from looking at it, it was done for the Karadzic case and the references to documents are -- have Karadzic 65 ter numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So we put on the last page in e-court a legend, so where we have Mladic 65 ter numbers we provide those for anyone reading that that wants to look to see what she's referenced. So I just spoke to Mr. Lukic about that and -- so that would be helpful, but that last page is an OTP product that we added on as a legend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me see. I have in front of me a list comparing the previous testimony, page numbers 40772 and 40773. Is that what you are referring to? In which I find 65 ter numbers for both cases. That's the one? Mr. Lukic, Mr. Petrusic, no problem with that I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then the witness has entered the courtroom again. Mr. Petrusic, are you ready to cross-examine the witness? Ms. Schmitz, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Petrusic. Mr. Petrusic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Schmitz, first of all, could you tell us what you did before you joined Medecins Sans Frontieres?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Well, I did my examination as a general nurse in 1984 and worked then in different hospitals until 1989, when I left with a German NGO called Kapagnenmor [phoen] to South Sudan. There I got to know MSF and so I switched to MSF and started with MSF beginning April 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: From 1989 through 1995 you were involved only with work for the MSF?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: No. Between missions I did also work as a nurse and I did also work in the office of MSF in Bonn partly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When did you arrive in the area of the former Yugoslavia for the first time as a nurse?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I did work in Croatia from March until June 1991 with MSF at the Dalmatian coast, and then I arrived on the 6th of June, 1995, in Belgrade in order to be deployed in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Before June 6th, between these two missions in Srebrenica and Dalmatia, were you in any other areas in the former Bosnia -- in Bosnia and Herzegovina, any other areas that were under threat?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I was not in any other areas of the former Yugoslavia. I was in other countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: We will get to that a little later. In one of the contacts that you describe as a meeting with General Mladic on the 12th of July - and you will remind me if I'm mistaken - but you said that you told General Mladic that you had helped Serbs in Zenica. I just want to jog your memory. Is this something that you actually said and did you ever go to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Well, I haven't said it correctly like this. What I did is I informed Mr. Mladic that MSF is working in other areas supporting Serbian population, and I never mentioned the place Zenica. Personally I have not been in any other areas of the former Yugoslavia, but colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 12 of your statement dated the 21st of March of this year, you say that there were two kinds of personnel that was necessary for the work of the MSF. Could you please tell us what personnel that was, personnel of the MSF, and were there any -- was there any medical staff there, local or people who worked for the Ministry of Health of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina. Could you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes. So the national MSF staff were 13 people who were employed by us and getting a salary and were needed to have a running mission. So, for example, a cook or a driver or a translator. Then the second category of national staff was the Ministry of Health's staff. I don't remember the exact figure, more than hundred medical staff employed by the Ministry of Health, who did work with us together and who got some incentive like hygienic products or some similar things like this. They did not get a salary from us because they were not MSF staff. That's a difference for us. They were supposed to receive their salary from the Bosnian Ministry of Health.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In the Srebrenica hospital, how many people of the medical staff had higher education; in other words, who were doctors, surgeons, war surgeons, and so on? What was the professional expertise of the staff there?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I -- there were five medical doctors, amongst them one surgeon, Ilijaz Pilav, but I do not know the level of education because Ilijaz, for example, who was the key person in the hospital, had learned most of his techniques, his surgical techniques, by working together with the international surgeons of MSF. So I don't know what degree of specialised education he had, but certainly there were five doctors who were studied medical doctors. And then there were lots of general nurses and paramedical staff and helpers and cleaners and auxiliaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: How was the hospital equipped? What kind of equipment did they have?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: What would you mean? Are you speaking about beds? Are you speaking about an X-ray? Are you speaking about the ICU? We didn't have breathing machines. There was one area which was called "ICU" but certainly not as equipped as an ICU here or, for example, in DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Well, compared to the hospitals that you've been to throughout your career since 1989, visiting various crisis areas throughout the world, where would you place this hospital in terms of their technological equipment and also medical supplies and medicines?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I would place the hospital on more or less the same level in any other war area, like Somalia or Chechnya, where I have been working in the hospital in Chechnya even in the OT. So there wasn't much equipment and often it had to be improvised. In terms of medical supplies, it was MSF supplying the hospital with the basics --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, the Chamber wonders relevance of these matters. So could you -- if it is relevant - I'm not saying it's not - could you please come to your point as quickly as possible so that we also understand what the relevance is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what is the probative value of knowing comparison with other war hospitals, where we have got no knowledge about so we can't even verify that? Would you please focus, first of all, on the most relevant issues because spontaneously all three Judges raised that same question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I shall accept your suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: At the meetings that you speak about in paragraph 13, in addition to the members of the UNHCR, ICRC, UNPROFOR, et cetera - these meetings were held at the post office - did you see any representatives of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or rather, the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I never saw any representative in one of these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Also you said that during the first few days of your stay in Srebrenica - that is paragraph 14 - you said it was relatively calm but you had the feeling that the town was an open-air prison. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: It meant to me that I felt that there was no freedom of movement. The population had to stay in Srebrenica. It was an enclave. People were not allowed simply to travel to Sarajevo. And I remember that the nearby enclave Zepa, our medical doctor carried secretly an examination table there, but they had to do that very secretly because they were not allowed to leave the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know that these two enclaves were separated, and according to the demilitarisation agreement no communication was allowed between the two enclaves?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I knew that these were two separate enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you know that these enclaves were supposed to be demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes, I did know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you know whether they had indeed been demilitarised?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: I certainly don't know anything about Zepa. In Srebrenica, first of all, I'm not completely clear about the definition of "demilitarisation" and -- so that's the first point. The second point, of course, I can imagine something about the definition. I did not know, not until the last day, how many weapons there were in the enclave, how many soldiers, how many fighters. That was all beyond my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Further on in paragraph 16 you say that the local authorities and the UNHCR informed you that there was a food shortage in the enclave and that people were starving.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have in e-court 65 ter 25214.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this, paragraph 1. Have you had a look?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and that's probably --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I have to say that this document dates back to four days before you arrived there, but will you agree with me that this convoy includes food supplies and also other supplies that were meant for keeping the hygiene of the population --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, if the witness knows anything about these convoys, we can ask her whether she has any -- if you want her to confirm that 6 tonnes of salt, 11 tonnes of beans, that that's food, then the Chamber -- the Judges of the Chamber can read and it's obvious that powdered milk, beans, biscuits, that that's food. So there's no need to ask the witness unless she has any personal knowledge about it, but to ask her to explain to us whether this document is about food is -- well, is - to say the least - superfluous, if not worse. Please proceed. Do you have any personal knowledge about these convoys, Ms. Schmitz?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My knowledge is that on 27 of June one convoy of UNHCR with food did arrive in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and whether that's the same as described here you wouldn't know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you proceed, may I ask, Mr. Petrusic, you said in page 42, lines 21 and 22, this document dates back to four days before you arrived there. I see the date of this document is 20th of June, 1995. The witness testified that she arrived on the 6th of June. Please clarify that. Ms. Schmitz.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I arrived on 6th of June in Belgrade. I arrived 24 June in Srebrenica only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- because negotiations took that much time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a very good clarification. Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Now that we're on the topic of humanitarian aid, do you know that this humanitarian aid that arrived through the UNHCR had been abused? Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: If it has been abused?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Had there been any abuse as far as the distribution of humanitarian aid was concerned? I mean, I seem to be leading now, but I'm saying: Was all of this aid sent to the civilian population or was some of it given to the military? Did you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: No, not at all. I believe UNHCR is in a much better position to explain. We did not monitor the distribution, which we sometimes do in other countries, but here we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have in e-court 65 ter 1D00076.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document under this number is not available in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 04638611 is the ERN number, so can you find it that way?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We can barely hear the speaker, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, the interpreters have difficulties in hearing you, so could you please speak perhaps a bit more loudly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document is 04638611.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While waiting for that, Mr. Petrusic, 25214, the document we looked at a minute ago, do you intend to tender that? If so, we could deal with it right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought I'd do it at the end, but I will accept that if you think it should be tendered now, then I am going to tender it now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Petrusic please speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you are again invited to speak into the microphone, Mr. Petrusic, by the interpreters. Madam Registrar, 25214 -- no objections, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number would be D11, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D11 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Ms. Schmitz, please, did you know that this convoy had arrived in Srebrenica on the 4th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: No. I would have to check again -- actually, I'm sure there was a convoy 27th June and there was a convoy arriving 13th July when all the population was gone. 4th July I do not remember at all, but I'm happy to check once more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, is this a different convoy or is it the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a different convoy, the 4th of July. The previous one was on the 28th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So this convoy now refers to the one on the screen. Put your next question to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the witness answered this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So did you know that this convoy had arrived?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTINE SCHMITZ
utterances.text: No. Did the convoy arrive in Srebrenica on the 4th? Because I should have known and I know only about the one on the 27th and on the 13th. The NGO community in Srebrenica was very small, so the UNHCR representative was living in our house. Therefore, I would be very surprised if the convoy did arrive and I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall tender this document. The number is ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D00076.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, do I understand since the witness says she doesn't know anything about this, that you asked about the convoy arriving. May I then take it that you want to bar table this document? Is that how we have to understand you tendering it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. The Defence will tender it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
